request.systemPrompt:
You are a requirements analyst for a URL shortener service. You read a raw
requirement (a feature request or a bug report) and normalize it into a
structured specification an engineering team can act on.

You must be honest about what the requirement does not say. Do not invent
behavior the requirement never specifies. If wording is unclear or leaves room
for more than one reasonable interpretation, record that in "ambiguities".
If the requirement is entirely silent about something the design will need an
answer to before implementation can proceed (not just unclear, but never
addressed at all), record that separately in "openQuestions" and do not guess
at a policy to fill it.

Respond with exactly one fenced json block containing an object with these keys:
- normalizedProblem: string, the requirement restated precisely and concisely
- acceptanceCriteria: array of objects, each with "id" (string like "AC-1"),
  "description" (string), and "riskLevel" (one of "LOW", "MEDIUM", "HIGH", "CRITICAL")
- ambiguities: array of strings, wording or scope that is unclear
- assumptions: array of strings, reasonable assumptions you are proposing to
  resolve an ambiguity (for a human to confirm or reject, not silently adopted)
- outOfScope: array of strings, explicitly excluded from this requirement
- openQuestions: array of strings, things the requirement never addresses at all
  that the design will need answered before implementation can proceed. Leave
  this empty if the requirement, even if imperfectly worded, actually covers
  everything the design needs.
request.userPrompt:
Here is the raw requirement:

# Requirement: faster resolution for popular links

Popular short URLs should be faster to resolve without hammering the database on every
request.

Right now every redirect does a database lookup. For links that get a lot of traffic,
that is unnecessary load: the mapping from short code to long URL basically never
changes once it exists.

Make popular links resolve faster.

response.text:
```json
{
  "normalizedProblem": "Introduce a caching layer for short-code-to-long-URL resolution so that high-traffic short URLs do not require a database query on every redirect request, thereby reducing database load and improving redirect latency for popular links.",
  "acceptanceCriteria": [
    {
      "id": "AC-1",
      "description": "A resolved short URL that is served from cache must return the correct long URL (the same destination a database lookup would return).",
      "riskLevel": "CRITICAL"
    },
    {
      "id": "AC-2",
      "description": "After a short URL is resolved for the first time (or re-populated into cache), subsequent requests for that short code must not result in a database query for as long as the cache entry remains valid.",
      "riskLevel": "HIGH"
    },
    {
      "id": "AC-3",
      "description": "If a short URL does not exist in the cache, the system must fall back to the database, return the correct result, and populate the cache for future requests.",
      "riskLevel": "HIGH"
    },
    {
      "id": "AC-4",
      "description": "If a short URL is deleted or its destination is updated, the corresponding cache entry must be invalidated so that stale mappings are not served beyond a defined maximum staleness window.",
      "riskLevel": "CRITICAL"
    },
    {
      "id": "AC-5",
      "description": "If the cache is unavailable or returns an error, the system must fall back to the database and continue serving redirects without user-visible failure.",
      "riskLevel": "HIGH"
    },
    {
      "id": "AC-6",
      "description": "Database query volume for short-code lookups must decrease measurably under load conditions representative of popular links (a specific threshold to be agreed upon, e.g., cache hit rate ≥ N% for links above a traffic threshold).",
      "riskLevel": "MEDIUM"
    },
    {
      "id": "AC-7",
      "description": "Redirect latency (p50 and p99) for cached short URLs must be lower than the current baseline latency that includes a database round-trip.",
      "riskLevel": "MEDIUM"
    },
    {
      "id": "AC-8",
      "description": "Short URLs that have never been requested, or that are below the 'popular' threshold (if selective caching is adopted), must still resolve correctly via the existing database path.",
      "riskLevel": "MEDIUM"
    }
  ],
  "ambiguities": [
    "The requirement never defines 'popular': it is unclear whether all short URLs should be cached uniformly or only those that exceed some request-frequency threshold, and if the latter, what that threshold is.",
    "'Basically never changes' implies mutability is possible but rare. It is unclear whether updates and deletions of short URLs are supported at all in the current system, which directly affects cache invalidation design.",
    "The acceptable staleness window (TTL) for cached entries is not specified—it is unknown whether stale-by-seconds or stale-by-minutes is acceptable.",
    "The caching technology or layer is not specified (in-process memory, shared cache such as Redis/Memcached, CDN edge caching, etc.).",
    "It is unclear whether 'popular' determination should be proactive (pre-warm cache for known high-traffic links) or reactive (cache on first miss).",
    "The requirement does not state whether analytics or click-tracking that currently happens during the database lookup must continue to work correctly when requests are served from cache."
  ],
  "assumptions": [
    "Cache-aside (lazy population on first miss) is the default strategy unless pre-warming is explicitly requested, since the requirement only describes reducing repeated database hits.",
    "All short URLs will be cached uniformly with a TTL rather than implementing a popularity-detection mechanism, unless the team decides selective caching is worth the added complexity.",
    "Cache invalidation on update or delete will be treated as a hard requirement to avoid serving wrong destinations, even though the requirement implies links 'basically never change'.",
    "The cache fallback path (AC-5) must be transparent to end users—a cache outage must not cause redirect failures.",
    "Existing redirect HTTP semantics (301 vs 302 status codes) are unchanged by this work; browser-level caching via 301 is considered a separate concern."
  ],
  "outOfScope": [
    "Changes to the short-URL creation or management workflows.",
    "Client-side or browser caching strategy (e.g., choosing between 301 and 302 redirects to control browser cache behavior).",
    "CDN-level caching unless explicitly decided as the implementation approach.",
    "Rewriting or optimizing any database queries beyond reducing how often they are called.",
    "Defining or changing the link-update or link-delete features themselves."
  ],
  "openQuestions": [
    "What is the maximum acceptable staleness for a cached redirect? (i.e., if a long URL is changed or a short URL is deleted, how quickly must all caches reflect that change?)",
    "Is there a popularity threshold, and if so how is it measured and enforced? Or should every short URL be cached on first resolution?",
    "Does the current system support updating or deleting a short URL's destination? If so, what is the current mechanism, and can it be hooked for cache invalidation?",
    "Is per-request click/analytics tracking currently performed during the database lookup? If yes, how should tracking be handled when the lookup is skipped?",
    "What cache infrastructure is available or approved for use in this environment (e.g., Redis, Memcached, in-process, CDN)?",
    "Are there compliance, privacy, or data-residency constraints that restrict where short-code-to-URL mappings can be stored outside the primary database?",
    "What are the concrete latency and cache-hit-rate targets that define 'faster' for the purposes of this requirement?"
  ]
}
```
